steps: Read a value: go up from one axis to the line, then across to the other axis.
Distance-time: gradient = speed; a flat line = stationary.
Speed-time: gradient = acceleration; area under the line = distance.
Check which quantity each axis shows before writing your answer.
method_card.title: How to Read Real-Life Graphs
method_card.content: Real-life graphs turn a story into a picture. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and a flat line means the object is stationary. On a speed-time graph the gradient is the acceleration, and the area under the line is the distance travelled. Split areas into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums, then add them. Conversion graphs are straight lines that swap one unit for another: read across, then up or down. Always keep the units each axis shows.
method_card.example:
A speed-time graph rises from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s, then holds 20 m/s for 10 s.

Triangle: ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m. Rectangle: 10 × 20 = 200 m.

Total distance = 250 m.

steps: The area under a speed-time graph is the distance travelled. Split the shape into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums.
Triangle = ½ × base × height. Rectangle = base × height. Trapezium = ½ × (top + bottom) × width.
Work out each region, then add them all for the total distance.
gold.title: Gold: area under a speed-time graph

example.question: A speed-time graph rises from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s, then holds 20 m/s for 10 s. Find the distance.

steps: On a distance-time graph the height is how far you have gone. Go up from the time axis to the line, then across to the distance axis to read a value.
A flat, horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary. Measure the width of the flat part in time.
Speed = distance ÷ time. Keep the units the axes use.
bronze.title: Bronze: read straight off the graph

example.question: A car travels 90 km in 3 hours. Find its speed.

steps: Speed is the gradient of a distance-time graph: change in distance ÷ change in time. Change minutes to hours first if the answer must be in km/h (30 min = 0.5 h).
On a speed-time graph the gradient is the acceleration: change in speed ÷ time, in m/s².
A downward gradient is deceleration; give it as a positive number.
silver.title: Silver: speed and acceleration as gradients

example.question: A car speeds up from 0 to 24 m/s in 8 seconds. Find the acceleration.

gold.hint: Split the area into a triangle, a rectangle, a trapezium and a triangle, then add.
gold.display: Find the total distance travelled for the entire journey shown in the speed-time graph.

guided_steps.hint: Half the two heights added, times the width.

guided_steps.say: One region left, then add them all.

guided_steps.done: They cover the full 20 seconds, so 280 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: The regions should span the whole journey.

misconceptions.message: The speed is not 20 for the whole journey. Split it into a triangle, a rectangle, a trapezium and a triangle: 40 + 160 + 60 + 20 = 280 m. Treating it as 20 × 20 gives 400.
The journey keeps going after 12 seconds. Add the slowing-down parts too: 40 + 160 + 60 + 20 = 280 m. Stopping at the rectangle gives only 200 m.

gold.hint: Split the area into a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle, then add.
gold.display: A speed-time graph shows a car speed up from 0 to 15 m/s over the first 5 seconds, hold 15 m/s until 15 seconds, then slow to 0 at 20 seconds. Find the total distance.

guided_steps.done: They cover the full 20 seconds, so 225 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: The regions should span the whole journey.

misconceptions.message: The car is not at 15 m/s for the whole 20 seconds. Triangle + rectangle + triangle = 37.5 + 150 + 37.5 = 225 m. Using 15 × 20 gives 300.
The speeding-up and slowing-down parts still cover distance. Add both triangles: 37.5 + 150 + 37.5 = 225 m. The middle rectangle alone is only 150 m.

gold.hint: Use only the first part: its distance divided by its time.
gold.display: A distance-time graph shows a runner covering 400 m in 50 seconds. For the first 20 seconds they ran at constant speed, covering 200 m. What was their speed (m/s) in the first 20 seconds?

guided_steps.hint: The metres covered in the first 20 seconds.

guided_steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time, using only the first part.

guided_steps.done: 10 m/s for 20 s covers 200 m, matching.

misconceptions.message: For the first part, use only its numbers: 200 m in 20 s gives 200 ÷ 20 = 10 m/s. Using the whole run, 400 ÷ 50 = 8 m/s, answers a different question.

gold.hint: Use the change in speed, not the final speed, divided by the time.
gold.display: A speed-time graph shows constant acceleration from 5 m/s to 25 m/s over 8 seconds. What is the acceleration?

guided_steps.done: Starting at 5 and gaining 2.5 each second reaches 25, matching.
guided_steps.hint: Add the gain back over 8 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Use the change in speed: (25 − 5) ÷ 8 = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 m/s². Dividing 25 by 8 forgets that it started at 5 m/s.

gold.hint: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.
gold.display: A speed-time graph is a triangle: speed increases from 0 to 30 m/s over 12 seconds, then instantly drops to 0. What is the total distance?

guided_steps.say: A triangle is half of that rectangle.

misconceptions.message: A triangle is half of the surrounding rectangle. Area = ½ × 12 × 30 = 180 m. Using 30 × 12 = 360 forgets the ½.

bronze.hint: Go up from 20 minutes to the line, then across to the distance axis.
bronze.display: The distance-time graph shows a journey. How far had the person travelled after 20 minutes?

guided_steps.pre: At 10 minutes, read up to the line then across. Distance (km) =
guided_steps.hint: Go up from 10, across to the distance axis.

guided_steps.done: The line sits at 6 km from 20 to 30 minutes, so 6 km is right.
guided_steps.hint: The flat part means the same height.

misconceptions.note: reads the x-axis value as the distance
misconceptions.message: Read up from 20 on the time axis to the line, THEN across to the distance axis. The distance is 6 km, not the time value 20.

bronze.hint: Find the flat part of the line, then work out how long it lasts.
bronze.display: Using the same journey graph, for how many minutes was the person stationary?

guided_steps.pre: The line first goes level at a time of (minutes)
guided_steps.hint: Where does the line stop climbing?

guided_steps.say: It stays level until the line starts climbing again.

guided_steps.pre: The line starts climbing again at (minutes)
guided_steps.hint: The next point where the height increases.
Subtract the start time from the end time.

misconceptions.note: gives the height of the flat part instead of its duration
misconceptions.message: The flat part is where the distance does not change. It runs from 20 to 30 minutes, so the stationary time is 30 − 20 = 10 minutes, not the distance 6 km.

bronze.display: A car travels 60 km in 2 hours at constant speed. What is its speed in km/h?

guided_steps.hint: It is given in the question.

guided_steps.done: Matches the 60 km, so 30 km/h is right.

misconceptions.message: Speed = distance ÷ time, so 60 ÷ 2 = 30 km/h. Multiplying gives 120, which would be a distance, not a speed.

bronze.hint: 10 miles is double 5 miles, so double the number of km.
bronze.display: A conversion graph shows that 5 miles = 8 km. How many km is 10 miles?

misconceptions.message: 10 miles is double 5 miles, so double the km: 8 × 2 = 16 km. Adding the extra 5 to 8 (giving 13) treats miles and km as the same size, which they are not.

bronze.hint: A horizontal line means the distance is not changing.
bronze.display: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line mean?

misconceptions.message: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary. Constant speed would be a straight sloping line.

bronze.hint: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so divide the distance by 60.
bronze.display: A walker covers 4 km in 1 hour. What is their speed in km per minute? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

guided_steps.hint: How many minutes make an hour?

guided_steps.say: Speed per minute = distance ÷ number of minutes.

guided_steps.hint: Use the calculator, round to 3 decimal places.

guided_steps.done: About 4 km in an hour, matching the question.

misconceptions.message: 4 km in 1 hour is 4 km/h. Per minute, divide by 60: 4 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.067 km/min. Leaving it as 4 keeps the units as km per hour.

bronze.hint: Think about speed × time, which is what an area multiplies together.
bronze.display: On a speed-time graph, what does the area under the graph represent?

misconceptions.message: The area under a speed-time graph is the distance travelled. Acceleration is the gradient (the steepness), not the area.

bronze.display: A bus travels at a constant speed of 40 km/h for 3 hours. How far does it go?

guided_steps.done: Back to 40 km/h, so 120 km is right.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 40 × 3 = 120 km. Dividing (40 ÷ 3) finds a speed, not a distance.

silver.display: The speed-time graph shows a car's journey. What is the acceleration during the first 10 seconds?

guided_steps.pre: At 0 s the speed is 0. At 10 s the speed (m/s) =

guided_steps.done: Speed rises by 20 in 10 s, matching the graph.

misconceptions.message: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time = (20 − 0) ÷ 10 = 2 m/s². Giving 20 is the speed reached, not the acceleration.
Acceleration is change in speed ÷ time, not time ÷ speed. 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 is upside down; the right way up is 20 ÷ 10 = 2.

silver.hint: Change 30 minutes into hours first, then divide.
silver.display: A distance-time graph shows a cyclist covering 15 km in 30 minutes. What is the speed in km/h?

guided_steps.pre: 30 minutes as a fraction of an hour =

guided_steps.hint: Dividing by a half doubles it.

guided_steps.done: 15 km in half an hour, matching.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply back by half an hour.

misconceptions.message: 30 minutes is 0.5 hours. Speed = 15 ÷ 0.5 = 30 km/h. Dividing by 30 minutes instead gives 0.5, which mixes up the units.

silver.hint: Distance is the area, which for a rectangle is height × width.
silver.display: A speed-time graph shows a constant speed of 12 m/s for 20 seconds. What is the distance?

guided_steps.done: Back to 12 m/s, so 240 m is right.

misconceptions.message: Distance = area = speed × time = 12 × 20 = 240 m. Adding gives 32, but the area of a rectangle needs multiplying.

silver.display: A speed-time graph shows a car accelerating from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. What is the acceleration?

misconceptions.message: Acceleration = (30 − 0) ÷ 6 = 5 m/s². The 30 is the speed reached, not how fast it built up.

silver.hint: A steeper line covers more distance in the same time.
silver.display: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line represents:

misconceptions.message: A steeper line on a distance-time graph means more distance in the same time, so a faster speed. Slower speed is a shallower line.

silver.hint: Deceleration = change in speed ÷ time; give it as a positive number.
silver.display: A speed-time graph shows a car decelerating from 30 m/s to 6 m/s in 8 seconds. What is the deceleration?

guided_steps.say: Deceleration = change in speed ÷ time (given positive).

guided_steps.done: Slowing by 3 each second from 30 reaches 6, matching.
guided_steps.hint: Add the loss back over 8 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Deceleration = change in speed ÷ time = (30 − 6) ÷ 8 = 3 m/s². The 24 is just the drop in speed, before dividing by the time.

silver.hint: Multiply the number of inches by 2.54.
silver.display: A conversion graph shows that 1 inch = 2.54 cm. How many cm is 8 inches?

guided_steps.say: Multiply the number of inches by 2.54.

guided_steps.done: Back to 8 inches, so 20.32 cm is right.

misconceptions.message: Each inch is 2.54 cm, so 8 inches = 8 × 2.54 = 20.32 cm. Dividing goes the wrong way, from cm back to inches.
